author: Claude (English teacher role)
basis: Shape: three short sentences of 7-12 words per slide, one or two words of 8+ letters, no participle clauses, clefts or fronting; subordinators (because, when, before) carry the logic. Every slide rewritten at all three levels against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. The workbook text passed on averages only: its A2 averaged FK 6.9 with 12 of 20 slides over the 20-second clock, and its A2 and B1 were largely the same sentences with harder words swapped in. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. Facts, order and every named item of the source are kept. Corrections, none silent: (1) slide 6 - the source's "poverty becomes less visible, but more powerful" is overstated; digital exclusion makes poverty harder to see, and nothing supports the claim that it makes poverty stronger, so only the visibility claim survives. (2) slide 15 - "floods, heat and extreme weather hurt low-income families first" is wrong about timing, because a flood reaches every house in its path at the same moment; the defensible claim, and the one the source means, is that low-income families are hurt hardest, lose more and recover more slowly. (3) slide 2 - "poverty is a system problem, not only a personal failure" hedges against its own point; rewritten as a fault in the system rather than a personal failure. (4) slide 20 - the source opens the closing slide with "Thank you for listening"; the house rule is to end on the claim, so the thanks is dropped and the slide ends on the claim. The workbook's "let us" (slides 1 and 20) becomes "let's". (5) slide 7 - the source's "health insurance" is named as Taiwan's National Health Insurance at B2, a precision rather than a new fact; A2 carries three of the four safety nets (social help, health insurance, emergency money) because of the clock, while B1 and B2 carry all four including local service centers. (6) slide 12 - "this improves English" is a claim about learning outcomes, so it is hedged to "tends to improve" at B2. (7) slides 11 and 13 - "elderly care" and "old people" are rendered as "older people", which slide 16 on dignity requires. Two source generalisations are kept but left hedged rather than sharpened, because neither carries evidence: that community groups find needs official systems miss (slide 9), and that financial literacy leads to safer choices (slide 10, where the source's own "education cannot replace fair wages" is kept).

slides.1: Good morning. Poverty is not always far away. Look around: a classmate skips lunch, a family works long hours, a student has no quiet place to study.
slides.2: SDG 1 asks every country to end poverty in all its forms. That is not only about income. It is health care, housing, education, and a fair chance to start again.
slides.3: Look at Taiwan. We have good schools and new technology, but not every family feels safe. Some struggle with rent, some with medical bills, some with jobs that never last.
slides.4: The first problem is working poverty. People work hard and still feel unsafe. Short contracts, low pay and long hours break their plans, and tired parents lose time with their children.
slides.5: Rent is the next weight. When it is high, families spend less on food, books and tutoring. Some students move house often or share one crowded room, where study is hard.
slides.6: Poverty also shows up online. Some students have fast internet, a laptop and parents who can help. Others share one phone, so a digital gap slowly turns into a learning gap.
slides.7: Taiwan has safety nets: social help, health insurance, and emergency money. They protect basic needs. But does that help reach us before a small problem turns into a crisis?
slides.8: Schools can soften the blow. Free meals, counseling, scholarships and after-school classes all help. A teacher who notices one quiet child early can change that child's whole year.
slides.9: Community groups help too. Food banks, social workers, religious groups and NGOs find people that big systems miss. Gifts alone are not enough, because real support builds skills and dignity.
slides.10: So what can we do? One answer is financial literacy. Students can plan a budget, save a little, borrow with care, and learn how to spot a scam.
slides.11: Data can help as well. Students can map what is missing near them: food, buses, care for older people, classes after school. But data should guide our kindness, not replace it.
slides.12: Service learning turns ideas into action. We can visit a local group, write posters in two languages, or teach younger children. We learn most when we work beside people.
slides.13: Taiwan is growing older fast. Many older people live alone and need care, money, transport, and help with their phone. Poverty follows health and family, not only pay.
slides.14: Migrant workers and new immigrant families need a fair door in. Language, forms and customs make help hard to reach. When a service is clear, the whole family can use it.
slides.15: Climate disasters make poverty worse. Floods and heat hit low-income homes hardest, because they have less money saved and fewer ways out. Climate action is part of this fight.
slides.16: Now, dignity. Help should never make a person feel small. If we only see weakness, we miss the strength that is already there, so we should listen first.
slides.17: To sum up, SDG 1 is about shared safety. Poverty touches learning, housing, health and dreams. Taiwan has support, but help must come sooner and reach further.
slides.18: We also need to drop the blame. Low pay, high prices, illness, family care, a flood: these push people down. Blaming is easy, but understanding is useful.
slides.19: You are young, but you can start now. Learn English and share these ideas, use data to show the problem, join a group near you. Together, small actions become powerful.
slides.20: So let's start where we stand. See poverty clearly, speak with respect, and act in our own school and community. A fair future begins with what we choose to notice today.
